Princeton University

At Opening Exercises, President Eisgruber encourages new Princeton students to value ‘what you learn along the way’

The ceremony marks the start of a new academic year for first-year students in the Class of 2030, incoming transfer students and new graduate students ahead of the start of classes. 

New graduate students welcomed to Princeton’s 'global community of scholars'

The incoming scholars attended a whirlwind of assemblies and events welcoming them to campus during Princeton Graduate School Orientation week.

Pre-read author Maryanne Wolf urges incoming class to read deeply, 'with courage and effort'

The Pre-read Assembly focused on Wolf's book, “Reader, Come Home: The Reading Brain in a Digital World,” which President Eisgruber selected for incoming students to read over the summer.

9/11 Service of Remembrance

In observance of this 25th anniversary of the 
Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, alumni and University officials will lead a campus Service of Remembrance at noon this Friday, Sept. 11, at the Memorial Garden between Nassau Hall and Chancellor Green.

The Memorial Garden and the annual service there honor the 14 Princeton alumni who tragically lost their lives. Prayers and readings will be offered by religious leaders from a variety of traditions. All are welcome to attend the ceremony.

W. Rochelle Calhoun to retire after more than a decade as vice president for campus life

Calhoun has played a pivotal role in enriching the student experience during a period of significant growth at Princeton. She will retire at the end of the 2026-27 academic year.

Princeton welcomes Class of 2030 that reflects continuing commitment to socio-economic diversity

“We are thrilled to welcome the great Class of 2030 and our newest transfer cohort to Princeton,” said Dean of Admission and Financial Aid Karen Richardson.

Incoming class hears call to embrace Princeton’s ‘bold and powerful commitment’ to free expression

President Eisgruber joined PEN America’s Summer Lopez *08 for his fifth annual Orientation session exploring free expression and ‘conversations that transcend polarization.’   

In banner ACS year for chemistry department, MacMillan and Chirik receive awards

MacMillan has been awarded the American Chemical Society's career Cope Award, Chirik the 2027 ACS Award in Organometallic Chemistry.

Eve Krakowski and Marina Rustow awarded grants from the National Endowment for the Humanities

The grants were part of a round of awards made to 81 humanities projects nationwide. The two Princeton grants are for projects connected with the University's Geniza Lab.

Princeton strengthens its support for AI and data science scholarship through Data and Intelligent Systems initiative

Tom Griffiths and Arthur Spirling are co-directors of the DaIS initiative, which builds on the deep links between AI and data science at Princeton while creating space for continued rapid progress in each of the fields.

Exceptional Faculty

Princeton faculty members are all exceptional scholars in their disciplines who are expected to teach as well as engage in research. Faculty work closely with undergraduates in the supervision of junior year independent work and senior theses.

Amir Ali Ahmadi

Operations Research and Financial Engineering

Ahmadi’s research formalizes decision-making through mathematics, creating tools that advance artificial intelligence, control systems, machine learning and data-driven discovery.


 

Yiyun Li

Lewis Center for the Arts

Li received the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for her memoir “Things in Nature Merely Grow” and has won numerous awards for her novels and short story collections. She teaches creative writing at Princeton.

Margaret Martonosi

Computer Science

Martonosi’s research on computer architecture and hardware design has fueled broad and lasting improvements in the performance, energy efficiency and security of computer systems, from mobile phones to data centers.

Simon Gikandi

English

A towering figure in the scholarship of the modern African novel and postcolonial literature, Gikandi brings a global perspective to the humanities. He is the founding director of the Princeton African Humanities Colloquium. 

Leslie Schoop

Chemistry

Schoop, a solid-state chemist, draws from chemistry and physics to find new quantum materials. She leads the Princeton Center for Complex Materials.

 

Howard Stone

Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering

Stone's fluid dynamics research connects engineering to chemistry, physics, and biology, with subjects including microdevices, swimming bacteria, flows of polymeric materials and respiratory virus transmission.

Chika Okeke-Agulu

Art and Archaeology

Okeke-Agulu is a celebrated artist, critic, curator and historian of African and African Diaspora art. He is director of Princeton’s Africa World Initiative.

Tom Griffiths

Psychology, Computer Science, Princeton AI

Griffiths’ research explores how studying AI can help us understand human cognition, and vice versa. His new book, “The Laws of Thought,” tells the story of using mathematics to explain how we think.

Tina Campt

Art & Archaeology, Lewis Center for the Arts

An innovative scholar of visual culture and a founder of Black European Studies, Campt explores the tactile and sonic registers of images and contemporary art. She fosters collaborative creative expression as director of Princeton Atelier. 

Arvind Narayanan

Computer Science and the Center for Information Technology Policy

Narayanan studies the societal impact of artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Anu Ramaswami

Civil and Environmental Engineering, PIIRS, HMEI

Ramaswami, who also leads the M.S. Chadha Center for Global India, pioneered the science of sustainable urban infrastructure systems and its translation to policy-making.

Elizabeth Ellis

History

Ellis works with archives and contemporary Native communities to illuminate lesser-known histories of early Indigenous America.

Frances Lee

Politics and Princeton School of Public and International Affairs

Lee’s research on Congressional politics and policymaking helps the public and scholars understand and address pressing issues in American democracy.

 

Agustín Fuentes

Anthropology

Fuentes studies the behavior, biology, and cultures of humans, our evolutionary ancestors, and other species we interact with, offering integrative insights that counter more simplistic narratives of the human experience.

Leonard Wantchekon

Politics

2023 Global Economy Prize winner Wantchekon came of age as a pro-democracy student activist in Benin. 

 

Marina Rustow

Near Eastern Studies and History

Rustow uses machine learning to decipher thousands of Arabic and Hebrew fragments preserved in a medieval Cairo synagogue.

Tracy Meyer, Princeton Graduate School
on Sept. 4, 2026, 1 p.m.

New graduate students gathered during Graduate School Orientation to be welcomed into Princeton’s “global community of scholars.”

Photo by
Denise Applewhite, Office of Communications

Hundreds of new graduate students filled Richardson Auditorium last week, where Princeton Graduate School Dean Rodney Priestley welcomed them to the Graduate School’s vibrant international community of scholars. 

Announcing that the Graduate School’s theme for the academic year is “Thriving as a Global Community of Scholars,” Priestley said that belonging to such a community benefits domestic and international students alike. “This theme was set four years ago,” he said, and “the importance of this theme has only become more apparent.”

“We live in an era of complex societal challenges that require us to think beyond borders and to recognize what we can learn from one another,” Priestley told the scholars. “The challenges we face now demand that we engage with one another.”

The 670 new graduate students will study in advanced degree programs across engineering, the social sciences, natural sciences and the humanities, including in the new Materials Science and Engineering Ph.D. program.

Addressing the assembly, University President Christopher L. Eisgruber said the graduate students are “critical to every aspect of what this university does, from teaching to learning to research and to service. You bring tremendous creativity, diversity and talent from throughout the world, and I am so happy that you are here.”

Eisgruber assured the new graduate scholars the University “will continue to stand up strongly for the principles that define us. We're going to stand up for academic freedom. We're going to stand up for free speech. We will stand up for scholarly quality, and we will stand up for diversity and inclusivity, values that are essential to the success of this and other universities.”

When Eisgruber speaks with lawmakers in Washington, D.C., he emphasizes the importance of attracting and developing new talent from within the United States and from around the world, he said. “I will continue to make the case for the talent that all of you represent.”

“At the same time that we confront political challenges today, we are faced with enormous technological change,” Eisgruber said. “Indeed, I think that the technological turbulence confronting us will prove over the long term to be more profound and lasting than the other challenges that get so much attention. We have to simultaneously seize the opportunities that artificial intelligence affords us while also addressing the challenges that it creates.”

The assembly opened two days of Graduate School Orientation events on Wednesday and Thursday, including panel discussions, fairs of student organizations and University offices, and social activities. Graduate School staff cheered and waved orange-and-black pom-poms as the students filed into Alexander Hall. 

Graduate School Dean Rodney Priestley told incoming graduate students, “You have joined a community that spans disciplines, cultures and continents. Pursue your work boldly. And help us demonstrate what a thriving global community of scholars can achieve.”

Photo by
Denise Applewhite, Office of Communications

‘One of the reasons that excellence is possible’ 

Priestley noted in his remarks that members of Princeton’s full graduate student body come from over 90 countries, bringing an “extraordinary range of experiences, perspectives and talents.” 

He traced the University’s roots as a global research institution back to its 11th president, James McCosh, who began 150 years ago to recruit faculty internationally and saw the number of graduate students from Europe and Asia grow. McCosh “understood that knowledge does not live within borders and that the benefits of scholarship belong to all humanity,” said Priestley, Princeton’s Pomeroy and Betty Perry Smith Professor of Chemical and Biological Engineering. 

“Fast forward to today and Princeton has become one of the world’s leading research universities,” Priestley said, “and the Graduate School sits at the very center of Princeton’s global identity.”

“Our ability to attract and educate outstanding graduate students from across the United States and around the world is not simply a reflection of our excellence,” he said. “It is one of the reasons that excellence is possible.”

“Ultimately, being a thriving global community of scholars is about impact,” Priestley concluded. “You have joined a community that spans disciplines, cultures, and continents. Pursue your work boldly. And help us demonstrate what a thriving global community of scholars can achieve.” 

Incoming graduate students asked questions of faculty and graduate student panelists, who offered scholarly and practical advice on pursuing success in graduate school. 

Photo by
Denise Applewhite, Office of Communications

Candid advice and a warm welcome

The morning’s proceedings continued with a panel of Graduate School academic and administrative deans who encouraged students to take advantage of the many kinds of support available to them, including professional development through the Graduate School’s GradFUTURES program. Students were invited to join in-depth breakout sessions scheduled over the next two days.

The deans were followed by a panel of faculty and graduate students, who offered scholarly and practical thoughts on success in graduate school. 

Erik Sorenson, the Arthur Allan Patchett Professor in Organic Chemistry, professor of chemistry, and the director of graduate studies for the Department of Chemistry, cited a book of speeches by 20th century Princeton president Robert F. Goheen. “As scholars, we only have one real obligation and that real obligation is to tell the truth,” Sorenson told the students. “So go and enjoy this splendid opportunity that you now have to go and find the unexposed truths in your fields — and enjoy the process.” 

Elizabeth Margulis, professor of music and acting chair of the Department of Music, also celebrated “the role of joy in the work that we do as scholars.” Margulis’s practical advice to students included joining multiple communities, developing communication and time management skills — and still expecting the demands of everyday life to derail their work at times. 

The three graduate students on the panel were candid about how difficult graduate school can be and offered wisdom and techniques for persevering through hard times. 

Alumni leaders then took the podium, showing off their Princeton jackets and welcoming the new graduate students to the larger community they now belong to. “We have 158 alumni associations around the world,” said Ryan Ruskin ’90, president of the Princeton Alumni Association, pointing out that graduate alumni make up 30 percent of all Princeton alumni. 

Natalie Berkman, who earned her Ph.D. in French and Italian in 2018 and is now president of the Association of Princeton Graduate Alumni, told the new students that APGA is here to help them make connections among the “extraordinary graduate alumni” in all walks of life: professors, scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, engineers, artists, diplomats, nonprofit leaders, and public servants. 

“While you're joining Princeton today as graduate students,” she said, “you're also building a lifelong relationship with a truly global community.” 

Emma George, a graduate student in the Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures, concluded the morning by teaching the audience the University alma mater, “Old Nassau,” and leading them in song. 

New graduate students connected with one another across disciplines during the Graduate Scholars Program Retreat.

Finding community

Prior to the two-day Orientation, 100 graduate students from three dozen departments attended the Graduate Scholars Program Retreat. The GSP is a peer-to-peer mentoring program hosted by the Graduate School’s Access, Diversity and Inclusion team. Graduate Scholars participate in social events and community-building activities throughout their first year. The day-long retreat on Tuesday gave students a chance to get to know one another and included a fireside chat with Raghuveer Vinukollu, who received his Ph.D. in civil and environmental engineering in 2011 and shared his reflections about graduate school and his career in industry.

Following Graduate School Orientation, on Friday, the Davis International Center held a half-day Graduate International Orientation. Students attended sessions on the nuts and bolts of maintaining their immigration status, payroll and banking in the U.S., and tax compliance.

The idea of “community” was threaded throughout the week’s activities and it resonated with the newly arrived students. 

Narjes Al-Zahli, a Ph.D. student in neuroscience, found the sessions in Richardson Hall inspiring, saying “I felt like the speakers deeply cared about our success and about us as people.”

Alberto Ortega Trejo, a student in the history and theory track of the architecture Ph.D. program, said he looks forward to learning from people in his field whose work he “deeply admires.” At the GSP Retreat, he also connected with students beyond his discipline. “I’ve met interesting people in plasma physics and electrical engineering,” he said. “It is very intellectually stimulating.” 

Maya Gambhir, who is pursuing her Ph.D. in computer science, had arrived at Princeton just two days before Orientation. Even on the first morning, “I felt that sense of community,” she said. “I think the student panelists were very vulnerable and very honest about their experience, and it made me feel more confident about my ability to succeed here.”

Rory Durso of the Graduate School Communications staff contributed to this reporting.

In Service of Humanity

Princeton University has a longstanding commitment to service, reflected in Princeton’s informal motto — Princeton in the nation’s service and the service of humanity — and exemplified by the extraordinary contributions that Princetonians make to society.

Christopher L. Eisgruber
President of Princeton University, Class of 1983

Connecting Learning & Service

The value of service is central to the mission of Princeton as a liberal arts university. It infuses the passions and pursuits of our students, faculty, staff and alumni, and is essential to how Princetonians serve the public good.

The University has reinforced its commitment to helping students and alumni use their educations to not only benefit themselves but also society more broadly. We push students, faculty and alumni to think about how their research, education and lives will benefit the nation, the world and humanity, and give them the support and resources to make it happen.

Leading Lives of Purpose

Princetonians pursue service in many ways, such as through a profession, vocation or role.

With innovation and purpose, our students work with each other to propose and pursue civic engagement projects throughout their time at Princeton. Opportunities for engagement arise in classes and research supported by the Program for Community Engaged Scholarship (ProCES), through student organizations and campus activities, and many have a home in the Pace Center for Civic Engagement. 

Our alumni engage in service across the world, participating in civic society and leading meaningful lives connected to a larger purpose and impact. Every year, more than 15,000 alumni volunteer to serve Princeton and University-sponsored projects. Alumni can serve with their class, regional associations, affiliated groups, the Association of Princeton Graduate Alumni and more. Annually at Alumni Day, top honors go to an undergraduate alumnus and a graduate alumnus for their service to society.

Building Community Connections

Princeton-sponsored service programs offer positive ways for students, faculty and staff to engage with the larger community.

Among many initiatives supported by the University community are opportunities to serve as firefighters; donate bikes, food and clothing for charities; promote sustainability and environmental stewardship; and host educational and commemorative events, such as for Martin Luther King Jr. Day.

At Opening Exercises, President Eisgruber encourages new Princeton students to value ‘what you learn along the way’

Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Email Print
By
Emily Aronson, Office of Communications
on Aug. 30, 2026, 7:44 p.m.

Opening Exercises marks the start of a new academic year before classes begin Sept. 2. Here, first-year students in the Class of 2030 and incoming transfer students show their residential college pride, including the Mathey College “moose.”

Photo by
Ryan Campbell, Office of Communications

President Christopher L. Eisgruber welcomed incoming undergraduate and graduate students to campus during the annual Opening Exercises ceremony on Sunday, Aug. 30, encouraging them to value the myriad opportunities to learn deeply and think critically while at Princeton. 

“As you enter Princeton, I hope that you will not hurry the journey at all,” Eisgruber told students seated on the lawn in front of Nassau Hall. “Give yourself permission to savor the experiences and the ideas that make this campus magical. Linger and reflect, because it matters profoundly what you gain along the way.”

Opening Exercises is a Princeton tradition that dates to at least 1802. The ceremony also includes readings from various faith traditions and the awarding of undergraduate academic prizes. In presenting the awards, Dean of the College Michael D. Gordin recognized the students for their intellectual curiosity, wide-ranging interests and superb academic accomplishments.

President Christopher L. Eisgruber welcomes incoming undergraduate and graduate students to campus during Opening Exercises, a Princeton tradition that dates to at least 1802. 

Photo by
Ryan Campbell, Office of Communications

 

The event marks the start of a new academic year for first-year students in the Class of 2030, incoming transfer students and new graduate students ahead of classes beginning Sept. 2. The high spirits of the afternoon were not dampened by a passing cloudburst, which gave way quickly to sunny skies. “We are going to keep powering through because you are the Class of 2030 and this will be memorable,” Eisgruber said as students cheered during the rain. 

As he began the ceremony, Eisgruber reflected on “how fortunate we are” to be on a campus that values the pursuit of truth, cherishes the importance of service and celebrates the rich tapestry of our community.

Students at the ceremony wear shirts representing each of Princeton’s seven residential colleges (left to right): Mathey, Yeh, Rockefeller, Butler, Huo, Whitman and Forbes.

Photo by
Denise Applewhite, Office of Communications

The enduring power of learning deeply and broadly

In his speech, titled “What You Learn Along the Way,” Eisgruber emphasized the enduring power of a liberal arts education to prepare students for whatever the future may hold. 

“Human advantage often comes from learning things without knowing why or how they will be useful,” he said. 

Deep and broad learning is essential, Eisgruber said, particularly in this moment when AI and other technologies are transforming society. He noted: “The easy availability of AI tools may tempt us to skip the journey that makes learning possible, but the capacity, and temptation, to replace learning with summary is nothing new.”

“So how can we know which knowledge or skills will be most useful in a world where technology changes with dazzling and dizzying speed?” Eisgruber posited to students. “The honest answer is that we do not know. But that is not new. It has been true for centuries, if not millennia, because one thing we do know, and have long known, is that the world will change in unexpected ways.”

“At Princeton, we want your education to equip you not only to succeed at your first jobs, but also to become leaders many years from now in a world far different from the one we now inhabit,” he continued. “Liberal arts universities like Princeton are based on the idea that you should learn both deeply and broadly, so that you will acquire not just knowledge but, more fundamentally, multiple ways of knowing that will enable you to discover, attack, and conquer questions that nobody has yet answered or even asked.”

Eisgruber said students “lose a lot” if they take shortcuts to learning new subjects. 

“Lectures, essays, and books travel an intellectual path. They are invitations to think along with the author,” he said. “As you know from the work that earned you a place at Princeton, scholarly exercise strengthens the mind. Conceptual details stimulate insight. Serendipitous connections among ideas launch discoveries and open new horizons.”

He added: “Genuinely understanding an argument or an idea is not merely a matter of repeating a conclusion; it requires your intelligence, your presence, your active participation in the train of thought. A good book or a good lecture is a journey, and if you take that journey you grow because of what you learn along the way.”

A brief cloudburst did not dampen students’ spirits during the afternoon event. The rain was quickly followed by sunny skies. 

Photo by
Ryan Campbell, Office of Communications

To close his remarks, Eisgruber harkened back to another Opening Exercises ceremony 45 years ago, when President William G. Bowen recited from C.P. Cavafy’s poem “Ithaka,” based on Homer's Odyssey. 

Inspired by the poem’s wish for a road “full of adventure, full of discovery,” Eisgruber told students that “It is not the degree you will earn, nor your post-graduation career prospects, it is not the endpoint, it is not Ithaka, but rather the marvelous, challenging, bewildering, sometimes uncomfortable and sometimes awesome journey that will be Princeton’s most precious gift to you.”

After the ceremony, new students walk in the Pre-rade behind Nassau Hall. 

Photo by
Denise Applewhite, Office of Communications

A robust Orientation week

After the Opening Exercises ceremony, the new students walked in the Pre-rade as students from Princeton’s sophomore, junior and senior classes cheered them on, joined by faculty, staff, alumni, family and friends. 

In the evening, Eisgruber led the annual Pre-Read Assembly in Jadwin Gymnasium, which featured a discussion on the vital importance of deep reading in a digital age with Maryanne Wolf, author of “Reader, Come Home: The Reading Brain in a Digital World.” 

The events were part of a robust week of Orientation activities, including a session on academic freedom and free expression held last week with Eisgruber and PEN America’s Summer Lopez *08.

Orientation also included three small-group experiences — Community Action, Dialogue and Difference in Action, and Outdoor Action.

Community Action, coordinated by the John H. Pace Jr. ’39 Center for Civic Engagement, introduces students to the University’s long-standing commitment to service.

Dialogue and Difference in Action provides opportunities to engage in critical conversations focused on community building and social action. 

Outdoor Action helps incoming undergraduates establish new friendships through activities such as camping, canoeing, biking and hiking.

Opening Exercises can be viewed on the University’s YouTube channel. The event will be archived online for later viewing.

Eisgruber welcomes incoming undergraduate and graduate students to campus during Opening Exercises, a Princeton tradition that dates to at least 1802.  Photo by Ryan Campbell, Office of Communications   The event marks the start of a new academic year for first-year students in the Class of 2030, incoming transfer students and new graduate students ahead of classes beginning Sept. 2. The high spirits of the afternoon were not dampened by a passing cloudburst, which gave way quickly to sunny skies. “We are going to keep powering through because you are the Class of 2030 and this will be memorable,” Eisgruber said as students cheered during the rain.  As he began the ceremony, Eisgruber reflected on “how fortunate we are” to be on a campus that values the pursuit of truth, cherishes the importance of service and celebrates the rich tapestry of our community. Students at the ceremony wear shirts representing each of Princeton’s seven residential colleges (left to right): Mathey, Yeh, Rockefeller, Butler, Huo, Whitman and Forbes. Photo by Denise Applewhite, Office of Communications The enduring power of learning deeply and broadly In his speech, titled “What You Learn Along the Way,” Eisgruber emphasized the enduring power of a liberal arts education to prepare students for whatever the future may hold.  “Human advantage often comes from learning things without knowing why or how they will be useful,” he said.  Deep and broad learning is essential, Eisgruber said, particularly in this moment when AI and other technologies are transforming society. He noted: “The easy availability of AI tools may tempt us to skip the journey that makes learning possible, but the capacity, and temptation, to replace learning with summary is nothing new.” “So how can we know which knowledge or skills will be most useful in a world where technology changes with dazzling and dizzying speed?” Eisgruber posited to students. “The honest answer is that we do not know. But that is not new. It has been true for centuries, if not millennia, because one thing we do know, and have long known, is that the world will change in unexpected ways.” “At Princeton, we want your education to equip you not only to succeed at your first jobs, but also to become leaders many years from now in a world far different from the one we now inhabit,” he continued. “Liberal arts universities like Princeton are based on the idea that you should learn both deeply and broadly, so that you will acquire not just knowledge but, more fundamentally, multiple ways of knowing that will enable you to discover, attack, and conquer questions that nobody has yet answered or even asked.” Eisgruber said students “lose a lot” if they take shortcuts to learning new subjects.  “Lectures, essays, and books travel an intellectual path. They are invitations to think along with the author,” he said. “As you know from the work that earned you a place at Princeton, scholarly exercise strengthens the mind. Conceptual details stimulate insight. Serendipitous connections among ideas launch discoveries and open new horizons.” He added: “Genuinely understanding an argument or an idea is not merely a matter of repeating a conclusion; it requires your intelligence, your presence, your active participation in the train of thought. A good book or a good lecture is a journey, and if you take that journey you grow because of what you learn along the way.” A brief cloudburst did not dampen students’ spirits during the afternoon event. The rain was quickly followed by sunny skies.  Photo by Ryan Campbell, Office of Communications To close his remarks, Eisgruber harkened back to another Opening Exercises ceremony 45 years ago, when President William G. Bowen recited from C.P. Cavafy’s poem “Ithaka,” based on Homer's Odyssey.  Inspired by the poem’s wish for a road “full of adventure, full of discovery,” Eisgruber told students that “It is not the degree you will earn, nor your post-graduation career prospects, it is not the endpoint, it is not Ithaka, but rather the marvelous, challenging, bewildering, sometimes uncomfortable and sometimes awesome journey that will be Princeton’s most precious gift to you.” After the ceremony, new students walk in the Pre-rade behind Nassau Hall.  Photo by Denise Applewhite, Office of Communications A robust Orientation week After the Opening Exercises ceremony, the new students walked in the Pre-rade as students from Princeton’s sophomore, junior and senior classes cheered them on, joined by faculty, staff, alumni, family and friends.  In the evening, Eisgruber led the annual Pre-Read Assembly in Jadwin Gymnasium , which featured a discussion on the vital importance of deep reading in a digital age with Maryanne Wolf, author of “Reader, Come Home: The Reading Brain in a Digital World.”  The events were part of a robust week of Orientation activities, including a session on academic freedom and free expression held last week with Eisgruber and PEN America’s Summer Lopez *08. Orientation also included three small-group experiences — Community Action, Dialogue and Difference in Action, and Outdoor Action. Community Action, coordinated by the John H. Pace Jr. ’39 Center for Civic Engagement, introduces students to the University’s long-standing commitment to service. Dialogue and Difference in Action provides opportunities to engage in critical conversations focused on community building and social action.  Outdoor Action helps incoming undergraduates establish new friendships through activities such as camping, canoeing, biking and hiking. Opening Exercises can be viewed on the University’s YouTube channel . The event will be archived online for later viewing.
